title: Shipping, tanker stocks rally as Trump launches Strait of Hormuz blockade
content:
[Oil Tanker]
HeliRy/E+ via Getty Images

The day's gains continued the "disruption" trade in which negative news surrounding the closure of the Strait of Hormuz rallies shipping stocks, while any momentum toward a resolution punishes them, TradeWinds.com noted.

Tanker stocks, which are especially affected by the Iran war, gained an average of 2.8%, according to TradeWinds, with clean product carrier names faring slightly better than the crude tanker group.

title: Strait of Hormuz oil tanker traffic blocked after Israeli strikes, Iranian media says
content:
[Oil Tanker]
HeliRy/E+ via Getty Images

Oil tanker transit through the Strait of Hormuz was halted [https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-04-08/oil-ships-hormuz-transits-blocked-after-lebanon-hit-fars-says] due to Israeli attacks on Lebanon, Iran's semi-official Fars News Agency reported Wednesday, potentially jeopardizing [https://seekingalpha.com/news/4573399-iran-may-exit-ceasefire-over-israeli-attacks-on-lebanon---reports] the ceasefire agreement.

Limited ship movement resumed through the strait earlier after President Trump announced a temporary ceasefire agreement, and Fars said two tankers were granted permission to pass safely through the strait.

Lebanon's Health Ministry said Israeli airstrikes Wednesday killed dozens of people and injured hundreds more, with rescue efforts underway to find others still trapped under rubble.

Israel's military said it carried out strikes aimed at Hezbollah hideouts, some of them in densely populated areas in Beirut; Israel said militants are moving from their traditional stronghold in the city's southern suburbs toward civilian areas farther north.

Even before the Fars report, Hormuz appeared to remain largely blocked, with shipowners trying to understand if they can safely transit the vital waterway.

Amid the uncertainty and confusion [https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/08/trump-iran-ceasefire-strait-of-hormuz-toll.html], energy-related shipping shares trade mostly higher, including DHT Holdings (DHT [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/DHT]) up 3.5%, Frontline (FRO [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/FRO]) up 3.3%, Dorian LPG (LPG [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/LPG]) up 3.3%, BW LPG (BWLP [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/BWLP]) up 3.1%, CMB.Tech (CMBT [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/CMBT]) up 3%, International Seaways (INSW [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/INSW]) up 2.9%, Scorpio Tankers (STNG [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/STNG]) up 2.1%, Teekay (TK [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/TK]) up 2%, Tsakos Energy Navigation (TEN [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/TEN]) up 1.4%, Torm (TRMD [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/TRMD]) up 1.3%, Teekay Tankers (TNK [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/TNK]) up 1%, Okeanis Eco Tankers (ECO [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/ECO]) up 0.9%, Ardmore Shipping (ASC [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/ASC]) up 0.7%, Flex LNG (FLNG [https://seekingalpha.com/symbol/FLNG]) up 0.4%.

"Should transits (to some degree) be possible in the coming two weeks, we might see a prioritization of emptying the Persian Gulf of its trapped tankers, before taking further vessels inside for new loadings," Fearnley analyst Fredrik Dybwad said [https://www.tradewindsnews.com/finance/shipping-stocks-fall-sharply-after-us-iran-ceasefire/2-1-1970598] in a note.

"Hence, this emerges as a risk for tanker rates should the trapped vessels exit and fighting escalate after a two-week period—as 10% of the compliant tanker fleet currently is trapped inside the strait," Dybwad wrote. "However, as a massive amount of barrels lie at port-side inventories inside the Gulf, a future scramble for tonnage in the case of a partial (or full) reopening of the Hormuz Strait will likely be positive for tanker rates... though we acknowledge this hinges on the strait not ‘closing’ after a short period of being open for business."

title: At least 20 LNG carriers stuck in Persian Gulf as demand soars - WSJ
content:
[LNG tanker ship]
Sky_Blue/iStock via Getty Images

At least 20 liquefied natural gas carriers - roughly half of the available global fleet available for charter - are trapped in the Persian Gulf [https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/us-israel-iran-war-2026/card/half-of-all-lng-carriers-trapped-in-the-gulf-brokers-say-huDGf773gO12FkvHLd6V], as demand from Asia surges, _The Wall Street Journal_ reported Thursday.

"The situation is dire and will have a lasting impact on the market, regardless of how quickly the conflict ends," GasLog COO Kostas Karathanos told _WSJ_; his company operates 34 gas carriers.

Ship brokers said the 20 ships trapped in the Persian Gulf comprise nearly half of all LNG ships currently available for charter, with rates rising to more than $200K/day from less than $98K/day before the start of the Iran war; the total global fleet is ~800 ships.

Energy traders expect LNG prices to rise by early next week, adding to this week’s 40% rise in Asia and Europe. “The effect on LNG shipping will outlast the conflict for a few months,” Karathanos said.

title: This may be the best way to play energy stocks if oil stays above $80 a barrel
content:
A focus on free cash flow could be lucrative for investors if oil prices remain moderately higher than they were in 2025. - MarketWatch illustration/iStockphoto

Updated with Tuesday’s closing stock prices and free-cash-flow yields, as well as the price of West Texas crude oil early Wednesday.

Since Feb. 27, the day before the U.S. and Israel began their attack on Iran’s government, oil prices have spiked, reversed and risen again. But at current levels, they support a significant increase in free cash flow for companies involved with oil and natural gas production, according to analysts at William Blair.

The continuous front-month price for West Texas crude oil CL00 on the New York settled at $67.02 a barrel on Feb. 27, the day before the conflict began. Then the WTI price spiked at $119.48 on Monday, before settling that day at $94.77. On Tuesday, WTI fell further, settling at $83.45. Early on Wednesday, it was up 3.4% to $86.30.

In a note to clients on Monday, before that trading session’s increase in crude oil prices was reversed, William Blair analysts Neal Dingmann and Bert Donnes said a “$15 move in oil can cause FCF yield to more than double.” This is based on the analysts’ coverage group of 17 small-cap and midcap U.S. companies involved in oil and/or natural-gas production or distribution.

In 2025, the average daily settlement price for WTI was $64.75. This year, through Tuesday, it has averaged $65.08. So a price of $80 a barrel supports the William Blair analysts’ thesis, and the price was well above that level Wednesday morning.

That information comes from the MarketWatch quote page, which includes a lot of information, and can be configured to show a long range for daily prices for commodities and securities. The data can be downloaded.

So now the important question is whether WTI can stay above $80. You might have a strong opinion.

FCF yield stands for free-cash-flow yield. A company’s free cash flow is its remaining cash flow after capital expenditures. It is money that can be used to pay dividends, buy back shares (hopefully to lower the share count and raise earnings per share), fund expansion or for other corporate purposes. An increasing FCF yield is typically a positive development.

A company’s FCF yield can be compared with its dividend yield to see if there is “headroom” to deploy more cash.

A screen of the 70 energy stocks in the S&P 1500 Composite Index XX:SP1500 shows the 15 companies with the highest trailing FCF yields, based on Tuesday’s closing stock prices and the past 12 months’ FCF per share. The S&P 1500 is made up of the S&P 500 SPX, the S&P Small Cap 600 SML Index and the S&P MidCap 400 Index MID. The data was provided by LSEG.

Pre-Market Stock Futures:

Futures are trading flat as we hit the mid-point of the trading week, and while we didn't see the snapback rally that was the star of the show Monday, at least all four major indices held their own as the conflict in Iran grinds on. The Nasdaq was able to eke out a tiny gain on Tuesday, closing at 22,697, up 0.01 %, while the Dow Jones Industrial closed down just 0.07% at 47,706. The S&P 500 ended the day at 6,781, lower by 0.21%, and the small-cap Russell 2000 ended Tuesday at 2,548, down 0.22%. Going forward, one thing is for sure: a speedy resolution to the conflict with Iran will immediately help oil prices retreat, and that will help keep the potential for higher inflation in check.

Treasury Bonds:

Yields moved higher across the Treasury curve as investors continued to monitor the impact of Middle East tensions on oil prices and to digest President Trump's comments on the progress and path of the military in Iran. The 30-year long bond closed the day at 4.79% while the benchmark 10-year note was last seen at 4.16%. With the Treasury Department continuing to buy back bonds, operations in early 2026 have targeted liquidity support in the 7-year to 10-year maturity sector. These ongoing buybacks are intended to improve liquidity in the Treasury market and manage government cash balances—not to reduce the overall national debt.

title: LNG tanker dayrates double to $200K in less than a day - Bloomberg
content:
[LNG tanker ship] 
Sky_Blue/iStock via Getty Images

Shippers are demanding more than $200K/day [https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-02/lng-tanker-rates-double-to-200-000-in-less-than-a-day-on-iran] for liquefied natural gas tankers in the Atlantic Basin, roughly double the amount obtained less than a day earlier, Bloomberg reported late Monday.

Those offer levels were at least triple [https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/daily-lng-freight-rates-jump-over-40-amid-mideast-strikes-spark-commodities-says-2026-03-03/] the previous assessed price for an LNG tanker by shipping firm Spark Commodities, which came in at $61.5K/day earlier Monday - which was itself up ⁠43% from from the previous day.

The surge in vessel rates has followed Qatar's shutdown of LNG production as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran began to spill across the Middle East region.

Transacted shipping rates - actual deals to lease vessels - are not likely to soar unless production cuts are prolonged in places such as Qatar and the U.A.E., Precision LNG Consulting's Richard Pratt told Bloomberg.
